clue.text: Swift work women learnt in translation in a day

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for women, as on clothing sizes or toilet doors

indicators.note: translating a text turns its words into a new form, so these letters are rendered in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A translator renders a work by Swift, done by women in a single day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in translation' rearranges W, LEARNT and A into WATERLAN, and D for day closes it. The second 'in' is only a link. Swift here is the novelist Graham Swift, not Jonathan.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterland is a 1983 novel by the English writer Graham Swift, set in the Fens.

clue.text: Pressed suit with old dictionary

parts.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with, as in w/
the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: Someone presses a suit while consulting an old dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressed suit' looks like ironing a garment; it means pressed one's suit, courting someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To press one's suit is to pursue a romantic courtship, which is what a wooer has done.

clue.text: Composer in back street makes journey

indicators.note: the composer's name sits inside the street abbreviation
back tells us to read the street abbreviation from right to left

parts.note: Maurice Ravel was the French composer of Bolero

explanation.surface: A composer living in a back street sets out on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the street abbreviation and 'in' holds the composer inside it. 'back street' reads as one phrase but splits into indicator and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who travels is making a journey, a plain synonym in the third person singular.

clue.text: He's in pub, backsliding after this, clearly

indicators.note: sliding backwards here means the whole assembled word is read in reverse, with a nod to relapsing
the man is placed within the word for pub

parts.note: a bar is a pub, or the counter in one
HE is taken as written; the apostrophe s stands for is, a link

explanation.surface: A man in a pub, slipping back into drinking, needs treatment before he is clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backsliding' reverses the pub with the man inside it. The definition plays on being clean: after a spell in rehabilitation one is clear of drink or drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehabilitation treatment is meant to leave an addict clean, so it is what comes before being clear of drugs.

clue.text: Upset spirit that shuffled about in the dark

indicators.note: about means the shuffled word goes round the other piece
shuffled tells us the letters of the word that are mixed up
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the spirit's letters run backwards

parts.note: gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: A troubled ghost that shuffled about in the darkness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reverses the spirit; 'shuffled' rearranges THAT into ATHT; 'about' wraps ATHT round the reversed spirit. The surface pictures a restless ghost.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the dark is being there after sunset, during the hours of darkness.

clue.text: Peer over large cape for comic effect

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the peer's title is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a lord is a peer of the realm
NESS is a word for a headland or cape, as in Loch Ness or Orford Ness

explanation.surface: A nobleman peers over a big headland for a funny effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses LORD to DROL. Peer looks like a verb, to look, but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Drollness is dry humour, the quality of being funny in an odd way.

clue.text: Older stars transformed Swift work

indicators.note: transformed means the letters of the two words are changed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Ageing stars are transformed by a work by Swift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transformed' rearranges OLDER STARS. This is Graham Swift's Booker-winning novel about four old friends.
explanation.definitionFit: Last Orders is Graham Swift's 1996 novel, which won the Booker Prize.

clue.text: Opponent of progress diluted fluid

indicators.note: fluid means not fixed in shape, so the letters of the word flow into another order

explanation.surface: A technophobe's watered-down drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fluid' rearranges DILUTED.
explanation.definitionFit: The Luddites were machine-breakers of the early 1800s, and the name now means anyone resisting new technology.

clue.text: Pantograph user creates squiggles round itself? Not in the morning

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go round the other piece
squiggles suggests wriggling lines, so the letters of the word are scrambled
not tells us to take away the letters for the morning

parts.note: itself refers to the definition, a tram being the same thing
AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning

explanation.surface: A drawing device makes wriggly lines round itself, but not before noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'itself' points back to the definition, a tram; 'Not' removes the morning from it, leaving TR, and 'round' puts the anagram ('squiggles') round TR. A pantograph is also the arm that collects current from overhead wires.
explanation.definitionFit: A streetcar, the American word for a tram, draws electric current through a pantograph on its roof.

clue.text: Swift's working at hotel in winter time

indicators.note: in places the working, at and hotel pieces inside the month

parts.note: JAN, January, is a time of winter
a machine that is on is working
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Swift is working at a hotel in winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the working, at and hotel pieces inside the winter month. The definition is Swift's first name: the 's makes it Swift's own.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift was the author of Gulliver's Travels, so the forename belongs to Swift.

clue.text: See 6
It qualifies grammatically, for instance

parts.note: a word that modifies a verb, and the word grammatically in the clue is itself an example of one

explanation.walkthrough: The clue works twice: this part of speech qualifies verbs, and 'grammatically' is one.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb is a word class that modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.

clue.text: Swift man's ear repelled by organ

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the word for ear is read backwards

parts.note: LUG is an informal British word for the ear
the liver is an organ of the body

explanation.surface: A Swift character's ear is put off by a musical organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repelled' reverses LUG into GUL. 'organ' looks musical but is the body organ. The 's means is: the Swift man is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemuel Gulliver is the travelling hero of Jonathan Swift's satire Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Such are the Houyhnhnms, in the author's estimation

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the run of words that follows, across the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Swift rated his rational creatures highly, in his own view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to a run hidden across 'author's estimation'. The surface suggests Swift's opinion of the Houyhnhnms, which is fair too: he set them above humankind.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's Houyhnhnms are a race of wise, rational animals of the equine kind.

clue.text: Found emigration tricky after money ran out

indicators.note: tricky means awkward, so the remaining letters are twisted into a new order
after here means once the money letter has gone, framing the removal that follows
ran out means the money letter has left the word, so it is removed

parts.note: M is short for money in economics, as in M1

explanation.surface: Moving abroad became hard once the cash was gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Without M, EMIGRATION leaves EIGRATION, which 'tricky' rearranges. 'Found' is the verb to establish, not the past of find.
explanation.definitionFit: To found something is to bring it into being, which is to start it off.

clue.text: Aids during 2 initial jobs

parts.note: to initial a document is to sign it with initials
posts are jobs or positions

explanation.surface: Help given while initial jobs are carried out.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 refers to 2-down, so the definition reads as aids during travels. 'initial' looks like an adjective but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Signposts are roadside markers that help travellers find their way.

clue.text: Judges new church not square in old city

indicators.note: not with in means the square letter is dropped and the other pieces go in its place

parts.note: Thebes was an ancient city of Egypt and of Greece
S is taken as an abbreviation for square, as in street signs

explanation.surface: Judges call for a new church, not a square, in an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: N and CH take the place of the final S of THEBES; 'not square in' signals the swap.
explanation.definitionFit: The bench is the collective term for judges or magistrates sitting in court.

clue.text: Martial piece, say, tackled by wayward genius

indicators.note: being tackled means being grasped, so the second piece is held inside the first
wayward means straying, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: EG, for example, is signalled by say

explanation.surface: A war-themed work, for instance, is tackled by an errant genius.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wayward' rearranges GENIUS to SIEGUN, and 'tackled by' sets the example abbreviation after its first two letters. 'Martial piece' sounds like a piece of music but is a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A siege gun is a heavy artillery piece used to batter fortifications, so it is a military gun.

clue.text: Cut misses out 2 swiftly

indicators.note: out means the word for misses sits outside the other piece

parts.note: gals are young women, misses
to lop is to cut off

explanation.surface: A cut is missed out, swiftly.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 refers to 2-down, so the definition reads as travels swiftly. 'out' puts the misses outside the cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse that gallops runs at full speed, so it moves fast.

clue.text: How one looks in new change of attire?

definitions.text: How one looks in new change of attire?

indicators.note: a change of means the letters of the word that follows are changed round

explanation.surface: How do you look in your new outfit?
explanation.walkthrough: N plus a rearrangement of ATTIRE ('change of'); the whole clue also defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in fresh clothes looks smarter or more stylish than before.

clue.text: Swift work met with fury

parts.note: a committee that met is one that sat
ire is anger, fury

explanation.surface: A work by Swift is greeted with anger.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift here is Jonathan Swift, the great satirist of A Modest Proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift wrote biting satirical works, so a satire is typical of what he produced.

clue.text: Milk supplier that is earning millions, when China's brought in

parts.note: a teat is what supplies milk

indicators.note: earning means taking in, so the millions letter goes inside the that-is letters

parts.note: IE, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A milkman earns millions when he brings in fine china.
explanation.walkthrough: 'earning' puts M inside IE. 'China' looks like crockery or the country, but the tea things come out at the hour of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: At teatime the tea service, the china, is brought out with cups and saucers.

clue.text: Swift place laid behind plant, say

indicators.note: behind places the second piece after the first
say tells us the plant's name is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a lily is a flowering plant
laid means put down, past tense

explanation.surface: Swift lays a spot behind a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' sounds out the flower's name, and 'behind' sets the word for laid after it. The place is the island of tiny people in Gulliver's first voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilliput is the island of tiny people in the first voyage of Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Swift German sheep jumps ditch? Not half

indicators.note: jumps suggests the sheep leaps round the other piece, which goes inside it

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep

indicators.note: not half means only one of the two halves of the ditch word remains

parts.note: a ha-ha is a sunken ditch bounding a park, invisible from the house

explanation.surface: A German sheep leaps a ditch, though not half.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a sunken boundary wall in a park, so taking half of it gives HA for 'jumps' to put inside RAM. 'Not half!' is also British slang for very much so.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Swift is the English novelist behind Waterland and Last Orders.

clue.text: Old man clipped bloomer

indicators.note: clipped means cut short, so the final letter is trimmed off

parts.note: gaffer is British slang for an old man, or a boss

explanation.surface: An old man has his flowers trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clipped' takes the final R off GAFFER. 'bloomer' suggests a flower but is British slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a blunder, an embarrassing slip.

clue.text: A man on board remains

indicators.note: on board means aboard a ship, so the man goes inside the ship letters

parts.note: SS, steamship, stands for a ship to be boarded
he is a male pronoun, a man

explanation.surface: A man who is on board ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is the old convention for inside SS, a steamship. Remains is the noun: what is left after cremation.
explanation.definitionFit: After cremation what is left of a body is its burnt residue.

clue.text: Swift beasts' house in backward Scottish isle

indicators.note: the house abbreviation is placed inside the reversed isle
backward means the isle's name is read from the end

parts.note: Soay is an island of St Kilda, home of Soay sheep

explanation.surface: The home of Swift's creatures lies on a remote Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns the St Kilda island into YAOS, and 'in' puts the house abbreviation inside it. The apostrophe of 'beasts'' is only a possessive link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yahoos are the brutish human-like creatures of Gulliver's fourth voyage.

clue.text: Swift sleeps and eats thus, served from trolley?

definitions.text: Swift sleeps and eats thus, served from trolley?

parts.words: Swift sleeps and eats thus, served from trolley?
parts.note: a swift, the bird, rests and feeds on the wing, and an airline meal comes from a trolley

explanation.walkthrough: Swift is the bird here, which spends almost its whole life airborne; airline meals are wheeled down the aisle.
explanation.definitionFit: The swift feeds and even sleeps while airborne, and food on a plane is served during the flight.

clue.text: Where 1's set iron poles

parts.note: FE is the chemical symbol for iron
N, north, is one of the two magnetic poles
S, south, is the other magnetic pole

explanation.surface: An iron set on poles.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 refers to 1-across, Waterland. The Fens are the flat drained marshland of eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Swift's novel Waterland takes place in the Fens of East Anglia.

clue.text: Magicians in Glubbdubdrib, terribly cross about rulers

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go round the rulers' letters
terribly means badly, so the letters of the word are mixed up

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is a ruling queen
a second ER, another queen, gives the plural

explanation.surface: Wizards on Swift's island are furious about the people in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges CROSS, and 'about' puts it round ERER. Glubbdubdrib is the island of sorcerers in Gulliver's third voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Glubbdubdrib is ruled by magicians who can summon the dead, so its people practise sorcery.
